title: LCIA Challenge Decision — Decision 1 (23/10/2017)
text:
DECISION RENDERED ON 23 OCTOBER 2017
Subject: The Claimant challenged the Sole Arbitrator (selected by the Parties from a list
provided by the LCIA) pursuant to Articles 11 to 14 of the UNCITRAL
Arbitration Rules 2010.
Outcome: Rejected
Seat: London, England
Governing Law of English law
the Contract:
Summary: The challenge related to: (i) the Sole Arbitrator’s experience and expertise;
(ii) certain procedural decisions; (iii) allegedly incorrect statements and
omissions in the Partial Award on jurisdiction; and (iv) the substance of the
Partial Award.
The LCIA Court rejected the challenge.
Given the Parties’ explicit choice of London as the seat of arbitration, English
law governed the determination of the challenge.
The Claimant’s consent to the Sole Arbitrator’s appointment was not vitiated
by any misrepresentations by the Sole Arbitrator. A claim made in the resume
of the Sole Arbitrator that the latter had “extensive experience of international
commercial arbitration under the major institutional rules ([including] LCIA
[and] UNCITRAL)” was not inconsistent with the Sole Arbitrator’s subsequent
admission of “not [being] familiar with the LCIA procedures when the
proceedings are under the UNCITRAL Rules”. Additionally, the record of the
proceedings showed that the Sole Arbitrator was knowledgeable about the
conduct of an arbitration under the UNCITRAL Rules.
In any event, the Sole Arbitrator’s alleged lack of familiarity with the LCIA’s
procedures as regards the form and format of awards when an arbitration is
conducted pursuant to the UNCITRAL Rules, and the purported failure to
highlight such unfamiliarity in the Sole Arbitrator’s CV circulated to the Parties
pre-appointment, do not give rise to justifiable doubts as to impartiality or
independence.
The Sole Arbitrator’s failure to establish a timetable for the entire case would
not be seen by a fair-minded and informed observer as displaying a lack of
impartiality or independence. Article 17(2) of the UNCITRAL Rules does not

require that the timetable cover the entire proceedings from the outset. It is
open to the tribunal and the parties to plan the first steps of the arbitration,
with the remainder to be left for subsequent determination.
The Sole Arbitrator’s decision to bifurcate jurisdiction and merits, where there
is no indication on the record that the decision to bifurcate was made
otherwise than in an impartial and independent manner, was a valid exercise
of the Sole Arbitrator’s discretion under Articles 17(1), 23(3) and 34(1) of the
UNCITRAL Rules.
The Sole Arbitrator’s decision to address, in the Partial Award, the merits of
claims that had been withdrawn, does not – in itself – show any lack of
impartiality or independence.
A decision or award does not have to list and summarise exhaustively any and
all communications between the parties and the tribunal, especially when
they are not directly relevant to the issue to be determined in the decision or
award.
The Sole Arbitrator’s alleged errors of law in the Partial Award do not support
a challenge absent showing that a fair-minded and informed observer would
consider that these aspects of the Partial Award give rise to justifiable doubts
as to the Sole Arbitrator’s impartiality or independence. It is not a function of
the LCIA Court to review whether legal or factual conclusions were properly
supported by the submissions and evidence.
The Sole Arbitrator’s statement in the Partial Award that the Claimant would
face evidential difficulties in proving its claim cannot serve as the basis for a
challenge where it was made clear that the Sole Arbitrator’s views were
provisional and an acknowledgment was made by the Sole Arbitrator that
there could be evidence to support the claim.
The mere dissatisfaction with the procedural decisions of an arbitrator is
insufficient to ground a challenge.
Decision 1 - 2

Decision 1 - 4

I. OVERVIEW
1. The Claimant has commenced arbitration proceedings against the Respondent in accordance
with the UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules (2010). The LCIA acts as appointing authority and administers the
arbitration. The Claimant seeks to be compensated for the termination, by the Respondent, of a
contract for consultancy services entered into in 2012.
2. This decision addresses the Claimant’s challenge of the sole arbitrator appointed by the LCIA
to resolve this dispute. The Claimant alleges that the arbitrator failed to remain impartial and to
disclose critical information pertaining to his ability to conduct the arbitration, and that he erred in
interpreting the applicable law to shield the Respondent from its liability. The Claimant requests the
immediate replacement of the arbitrator, as well as the partial refund of the fees paid to him so far.
3. The undersigned, […], after careful consideration of the facts, the law applicable to the
challenge, and the parties’ submissions, concludes that none of the grounds raised by the Claimant in
support of his challenge gives rise to justifiable doubts as to the arbitrator’s impartiality or
independence. The challenge is therefore dismissed. The costs of the challenge are deferred, and are
to be determined and apportioned by the arbitrator in his Final Award or in another decision.
II. FACTUAL BACKGROUND
A. The Parties
4. The Claimant is […] a […] national residing in the United States. The Claimant is not
represented by external counsel for the purpose of this challenge.
5. The Respondent is [...] a […] firm incorporated under the laws of England and Wales. The
Respondent is represented in this arbitration by [A].
Decision 1 - 5

B. The Underlying Dispute
6. In December 2011, the Respondent undertook to provide consultancy services to [a bank] ([Z
Bank]), to enhance the private sector development impact of its operations (the Project). To fulfill this
contract, the Respondent hired the Claimant as a consultant to provide advisory services related to
the Project and to lead its technical delivery in consultation with the Respondent and [Z Bank]. To this
effect, in January 2012, the parties signed a [contract] (the Agreement), for a term of two years
starting in February 2012.
7. The Agreement is governed by the laws of England and Wales, as provided in Article 24 and
Schedule 3. The Agreement also contains an arbitration clause, found in Article 25, entitled
“Arbitration”:
a) Any claim or dispute between the Parties arising out of or in connection with this
Contract shall be referred to arbitration in accordance with the arbitration rules
referred to in Schedule 3.
b) The decision of the arbitrator(s) shall be final and binding on both Parties.
8. Schedule 3 of the Agreement, entitled “Special Conditions”, modifies Article 25 as follows:
Any dispute, controversy, or claim arising out of or relating to this Contract, or the breach,
termination, or invalidity thereof, shall be settled by arbitration in accordance with the
UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules as at present in force.
9. Pursuant to Article 1(2) of the UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules, and by agreement of the parties,
the 2010 version of these Rules (the Rules) applies to this case.
10. It appears that in October 2012, representatives of [Z Bank] raised concerns about the
Claimant’s performance. On 21 October 2012, the Respondent suspended the Claimant pursuant to
Decision 1 - 6

Article 18(a) of the Agreement1, on the basis that [Z Bank] had “withdrawn its approval of [him] as
Team Leader”. On 24 October 2012, [Z Bank] confirmed to the Respondent that the Claimant’s
approval had been revoked. The same day, the Respondent informed the Claimant that the Agreement
was terminated with immediate effect, relying again on Article 18(a).
11. Since then, the Claimant has vigorously challenged this termination. On 5 December 2012,
counsel on his behalf served a Notice of Arbitration on the Respondent and tried to compel an
arbitration in [a country different to that of the seat of arbitration]. However, in October 2013, a
[State] court decided that the arbitration should take place in London. In May 2016, the Claimant
initiated the within arbitration proceedings. Upon the Respondent’s request, the Claimant prepared a
new Notice of Arbitration, dated 28 August 2016 but filed on 3 September 2016.
12. In this Notice of Arbitration, the Claimant alleges a breach of contract and seeks payment of
outstanding fees and expenses under the Agreement, for a total of USD 318,600. He also seeks
reputational damages, damages for distress and disappointment, and the refund of his legal fees and
the costs of the arbitration.
13. In its Response to the Notice of Arbitration, dated 3 October 2016, the Respondent states that
the claim is “misconceived and should be summarily dismissed”; that it is “ill founded and has no basis
in fact or in law and should be determined summarily as soon as possible”.
1 Article 18(a) reads as follows: “[The Respondent] may, at its sole discretion, suspend or terminate this Contract
at any time by so notifying the Consultant in the event that the Client or the Recipient at any time withdraws its
approval to the appointment of the Consultant hereunder or the Client suspends the Main Contract or
terminates the Main Contract or the Main Contract is suspended or terminated otherwise than by [the
Respondent] (as appropriate)”.
Decision 1 - 7

14. The parties agreed that London would be the seat of the arbitration and that the matter would
be determined by a sole arbitrator2. The parties designated the LCIA as appointing authority pursuant
to Article 6(1) of the Rules. On 8 December 2016, the LCIA appointed [the Sole Arbitrator]. As
mentioned in the overview, the parties agreed that the LCIA would administer the arbitration
proceedings.
15. The Claimant filed a Revised Statement of Claims, dated 20 December 2016, in which he raised
four “counts”: (i) breach of contract / wrongful termination, (ii) employment discrimination,
(iii) defamation / libel, and (iv) intentional infliction of emotional distress / outrageous conduct. In
addition to the relief sought in his initial Notice of Arbitration, the Claimant requested an unspecified
amount of punitive damages.
16. In the months following these initial filings, the parties and the sole arbitrator exchanged
numerous emails and letters regarding the conduct of the proceedings. These exchanges are central
to the Claimant’s challenge, and it is thus helpful briefly to summarize the most important ones.
17. On 21 December 2016, the Respondent asked the sole arbitrator to set a timetable for the
remainder of the case and advised that it would apply for security for costs. The Claimant replied that
he wanted the case to proceed as swiftly as possible. On 22 December 2016, the sole arbitrator
indicated that he would set a timetable and that his provisional opinion was to deny any request for
security for costs. He also urged the Claimant to retain English counsel to assist him in the matter. He
reiterated this advice on 13 January 2017.
2 Notice of Arbitration, 28 August 2016, Introduction and para. 58; Response to the Notice of Arbitration,
3 October 2016, at para. 27.
Decision 1 - 8

18. On 16 January 2017, the sole arbitrator raised again the issue of representation and (without
making any recommendation) identified barristers’ chambers in London that might be able to
represent him. He also explained that it was necessary to clarify his jurisdiction before proceeding on
the merits. The same day, the Claimant indicated that he was “temporarily suspend[ing] [his]
participation in this arbitration” due to his concerns regarding the fairness of the process and his
disagreement regarding the scope of the arbitrator’s jurisdiction.
19. On 17 January 2017, the sole arbitrator clarified that he had not made any findings regarding
the admissibility of the claims, and that it was his “right (if not [his] duty) to flag up such concerns [as
to jurisdiction], and to ask the Respondent for comments”. He also suggested holding a conference
call with the parties to avoid any further misunderstandings. The same day, the Respondent confirmed
that it would challenge the arbitrator’s jurisdiction with respect to the last three grounds raised in the
Revised Statement of Claims, and that it was reserving its right to apply for security for costs.
20. On 19 January 2017, the sole arbitrator held a conference call with the parties to discuss
procedural issues. Subsequently, the sole arbitrator sent a draft Procedural Order to the parties and
asked for their comments. Having received no such comment, on 23 January 2017, the sole arbitrator
issued Procedural Order No. 1 (PO 1), under which he directed, inter alia, that:
(a) the Revised Statement of Claims would stand as the Statement of Claim for
the purpose of Article 20 of the Rules;
(b) the Respondent would serve its Statement of Defence in respect of those
claims to which no pleas to jurisdiction were made on 16 February 2017, in
accordance with Article 21 of the Rules, and would simultaneously file its
pleas as to jurisdiction in accordance with Article 23(2) of the Rules.
Decision 1 - 9

21. Paragraph 3 of PO 1 addressed the manner in which the jurisdictional questions would be
dealt with. It reads as follows:
The Tribunal will consider whether to determine the jurisdictional pleas as a preliminary
matter or in its final award, in accordance with Art 23.3 of the Rules, within 7 days of receipt
of the Defence and Plea to Jurisdiction served in accordance with Direction no. 2 above.
22. On 24 January 2017, the Claimant asked whether he would be able to respond to the
Respondent’s arguments on jurisdiction and on the merits. The arbitrator replied, clarifying that he
would make sure to consider the Claimant’s views. Shortly thereafter, the Claimant retained English
solicitors to represent him in the arbitration.
23. On 21 February 2017, the Respondent served a Statement of Defense and Challenge to
Jurisdiction, in which it objected to the arbitrator’s jurisdiction over all claims except breach of
contract on the grounds that (i) they were not raised in the initial Notice of Arbitration as required by
Article 3(3) of the Rules, and (ii) the claims relying on the Employment Rights Act 1996, c. 18, or the
Equality Act 2010, c. 15, fell outside the ambit of the arbitration clause.
24. On 23 February 2017, the Claimant sought clarification from the sole arbitrator as to the
deadline to file his reply to the jurisdictional challenge. The arbitrator suggested a deadline around
mid-March, but said that justifiable extension requests would be granted. Indeed, on 24 March 2017,
the arbitrator granted a request by the Claimant to file his reply in April.
25. On 21 April 2017, the Claimant served his Response to the Statement of Defence and
Challenge to Jurisdiction, in which he withdrew his claims for defamation and intentional infliction of
emotional distress, but maintained those for breach of contract and discrimination. The Claimant
contended that the latter claims were submitted to the Tribunal in due time and were within the ambit
of the arbitration clause.
Decision 1 - 10

26. On 21 April 2017, the sole arbitrator informed the parties that he intended to rule on the
jurisdictional challenge first, without a hearing. It appears that the parties did not take issue with his
decision at that point. On 2 May 2017, the Respondent reiterated its position as to the jurisdictional
issues and requested its costs in respect of the claims withdrawn by Claimant, as well as security for
the costs of the arbitration pursuant to Article 26(3)(b) of the Rules.
27. On 3 May 2017, the sole arbitrator denied the Respondent’s request for security for costs and
indicated that he would proceed to rule on the jurisdictional challenge. On 9 May 2017, the Claimant
made additional written submissions on the jurisdictional issues as well as the Respondent’s cost claim
in respect of the claims he had withdrawn. On 8 June 2017, the sole arbitrator confirmed that he
would proceed to issue his award on jurisdiction.
28. On or about 19 June 2017, the Claimant informed the sole arbitrator that his counsel had
unilaterally decided to terminate his representation of the Claimant in this case. The Claimant also
questioned the reasons for the sole arbitrator’s decision to bifurcate the proceedings. On 25 June
2017, he asked the arbitrator to “bring this case to a closure” and to rule summarily on both the
jurisdictional issues and the merits of the case. With respect to bifurcation, the Claimant wrote that
he “would have preferred a single ruling adjudicating the entire case”.
29. On 27 June 2017, the sole arbitrator wrote to the parties. He stated that he had finished his
draft award dealing with the issues of jurisdiction. In response to the Claimant’s email of 25 June 2017,
he confirmed that his draft award was not dispositive of all pending issues in the case. With respect
to the merits, the sole arbitrator said that he was unaware of any agreement between the parties that
he should resolve any remaining issues summarily, on the basis of documents only.
Decision 1 - 11

30. On 28 June 2017, the Respondent communicated its understanding that the sole arbitrator
would deal with issues of jurisdiction on a summary basis, and nothing else other than a proposed
timetable leading to a hearing. On that same day, the sole arbitrator indicated that this reflected his
understanding, adding: “The Partial Award will be transmitted today along with a suggested timetable
to conclusion.”
31. Shortly thereafter, the Claimant advised that the email exchanges just summarized did not
reflect his understanding. He said he opposed the making of a jurisdictional ruling at that juncture, to
be followed by a hearing to deal with the merits. He added that the sole arbitrator was in a position
to rule on both jurisdiction and merits without further hearings. He concluded by lamenting the fact
that there were still, at that late stage, differing understandings of the process. In response, the sole
arbitrator stated that he considered himself entitled to rule on jurisdictional issues in any way he
considered appropriate, adding that he would issue his award on jurisdiction the next day.
32. On 12 July 2017, the LCIA notified the sole arbitrator’s partial award to the parties (the Partial
Award). In this award, the arbitrator formally recorded the withdrawal of the claims for
defamation/libel and for intentional infliction of emotional distress/outrageous conduct. The sole
arbitrator added that had the Claimant not done so, he would have dismissed these claims for reasons
which the sole arbitrator proceeded to set out in the Partial Award. The sole arbitrator also rejected
the claims for discrimination and punitive damages on the ground that he lacked jurisdiction. In the
alternative, he stated that he would have exercised his discretion to disallow the claims, on grounds
stated in the Partial Award. In the result, he confined the Claimant’s claim to one for breach of
contract, to be determined in a subsequent award following a hearing.
33. As regards the breach of contract claim, the sole arbitrator wrote, at paragraph 65 of his
Partial Award:
Decision 1 - 12

Though I have made no findings on the breach of contract claim, I believe it is only fair to [the
Claimant] to make it known that my provisional view is that this claim has some considerable
difficulties in terms of establishing the precise basis for the breach of contract as a matter of
English law. I believe that he is going to meet some considerable evidential difficulties in this
regard. I say that now, because I do not regard my function as arbitrator as one of surprising
either party in the final result. But equally, I make clear that my view is provisional, and there
may well be evidence that supports the breach of contract claim.
34. In an email dated 13 July 2017, the arbitrator wrote that he was proposing to set a timetable
to address the remaining claim for breach of contract. His email goes on to explain that he was not
able to do so earlier as he wanted to have the Partial Award sent out first to the parties. He then
added: “I was admittedly not familiar with the LCIA procedures when the proceedings are under the
UNCITRAL Rules.”
C. The Challenge
35. By email dated 27 July 2017, the Claimant submitted a “notice of challenge of the sole
arbitrator and request f[o]r his replacement” (the Notice of Challenge), pursuant to Articles 11 to 14
of the Rules and Articles 23 and 24(1)(a)(b)(d) of the UK Arbitration Act 1996, c. 23 (the Act). The
Claimant’s Challenge is based on “the sole arbitrator’s impartiality (sic), his failure to disclose critical
information pertaining to his ability to conduct arbitration under LCIA and UNCITRAL Rules and his
erroneous interpretation of UK laws to shield the Respondent from his responsibilities”. These
grounds are more fully set out below, in part III of this decision.
36. On 28 July 2017, the sole arbitrator wrote to the LCIA to advise that he did not wish to
withdraw from the case unless the Respondent agreed to the challenge. The sole arbitrator also made
three early comments on the challenge, which are summarized below. The same day, the Respondent
informed the LCIA that it did not support the challenge.
37. On 30 July 2017, the Claimant confirmed his intention to pursue the challenge. On the same
day, the LCIA informed the parties that the challenge would be submitted to the LCIA Court for
Decision 1 - 13

determination upon receipt of the outstanding deposit, directed on 5 July 2017. The receipt of the
above-mentioned deposit was acknowledged by the LCIA on 8 August 2017.
38. On 14 August 2017, the Claimant reiterated his concerns with the impartiality of the
proceedings and also raised some concerns with the costs of the arbitration thus far. On 15 and
16 August 2017, the Respondent noted again that it did not support the Claimant’s application and
that it did “not propose to participate in the challenge”. On 17 August 2017, the sole arbitrator sent
brief additional comments to the parties.
39. On 31 August 2017, the parties and the sole arbitrator were notified that pursuant to
Article D.3(b) of the Constitution of the LCIA Court, the LCIA had appointed the undersigned, […], to
determine the challenge.
40. On 6 September 2017, the undersigned invited the Respondent and sole arbitrator to file
additional comments before 14 September, if they so wished, and indicated that the Claimant would
have the opportunity to submit his own comments by 21 September 2017. On the same day, the
Claimant confirmed his agreement with this timetable. On 7 September 2017, the sole arbitrator and
the Respondent advised that they had no further comments to make.
41. On 8 September 2017, the undersigned acknowledged these replies and directed the Claimant
to submit his comments, if any, before 14 September. On 13 September, the Claimant submitted
additional comments amplifying or reiterating the grounds previously articulated in support of the
challenge. The undersigned acknowledged receipt of this email on 13 September 2017 and, subject to
the sole arbitrator or the Respondent having any additional comment to make, stated that he would
proceed with the determination of the challenge as soon as notified that the LCIA was in requisite
Decision 1 - 14

funds. The same day, the sole arbitrator made a brief additional comment on the challenge in reply to
the Claimant’s most recent email.
III. SUMMARY OF SUBMISSIONS
42. The Claimant has submitted various grounds for the challenge in his application dated 27 July
2017, as reiterated and amplified in subsequent emails (A). The sole arbitrator has briefly commented
on the Claimant’s submissions in several emails (B). The Respondent has chosen not to participate in
the challenge, having made clear at the outset that it opposed it (C).
43. The Claimant’s and the sole arbitrator’s submissions are summarized below. This summary is
provided by way of background only and is subject to the full submissions provided, all of which have
been carefully considered.
A. Grounds for the Challenge
44. The Claimant makes multiple allegations in support of his challenge. These allegations can be
grouped into four categories.
45. First, the Claimant states that his consent to the arbitrator’s appointment was vitiated
because it was based on misrepresentations regarding the sole arbitrator’s ability to conduct the
arbitration under the Rules. The Claimant contrasts the arbitrator’s email of 13 July 2017, where he
indicated that “he was admittedly not familiar with the LCIA procedures when the proceedings are
under the UNCITRAL Rules”, with the arbitrator’s résumé, in which he claimed having “extensive
experience of international commercial arbitration under the major institutional rules ([including] LCIA
[and] UNCITRAL)”.
Decision 1 - 15

46. Second, the Claimant contends that the sole arbitrator failed to treat the parties equally and
with impartiality in his procedural decisions. More specifically, the Claimant alleges that the sole
arbitrator:
(a) failed to establish a procedural order setting the timetable of the entire case,
in accordance with Article 17(2) of the Rules;
(b) failed to rule summarily on the matter, contrary to the parties’ wishes, as
expressed in the Respondent’s Response and the Claimant’s many emails;
(c) appears to have colluded with the Respondent, since the latter initially asked
that the case be summarily dismissed in its entirety, before agreeing to a
bifurcation after this course of action was proposed by the sole arbitrator;
(d) has a predetermined mindset to award the case to the Respondent, as shown
by his failure to take into account the Claimant’s opinion, by deciding on
3 May 2017, that the jurisdictional issue would be resolved in the form of a
formal reasoned award; and
(e) wasted the parties’ resources by addressing grounds already withdrawn by
the Claimant while refusing to rule on the substance of the Claimant’s case.
47. Third, the Claimant alleges that the sole arbitrator made incorrect statements in his Partial
Award, or failed to mention some of the Claimant’s arguments, thus acting contrary to Article 17 of
the Rules, notably by:
(a) incorrectly stating that the Claimant terminated the services of his attorney,
whereas in fact the attorney withdrew from the case;
Decision 1 - 16

(b) failing to reflect the Claimant’s concerns regarding the proceedings, by ending
his account of the procedural history in the Partial Award on 8 June 2017,
whereas the Claimant continued to raise concerns until 12 July 2017; and
(c) recounting the Respondent’s requests for sanctions while failing to mention
similar requests made by the Claimant.
48. Fourth, the Claimant contends that the sole arbitrator made errors of substance in his Partial
Award. More specifically, it is alleged by the Claimant that the sole arbitrator:
(a) intentionally distorted UK employment laws and overlooked both established
precedent (Lawson v. Serco, [2006] UKHL 3) and the substance of the
Agreement to shield the Respondent from responsibility and deprive the
Claimant from justice, by finding that the Claimant was not engaged under a
contract of employment with the Respondent and that he could not benefit
from the protections afforded by UK law due to the location of his
employment and/or his nationality; and
(b) prejudged the merits of the Claimant’s case, without any substantive
reasoning, by expressing at paragraph 65 of his Partial Award the provisional
view that the Claimant’s breach of contract claim has “considerable
difficulties in terms of establishing the precise basis for the breach of contract
as a matter of English law.”
49. The Claimant also reiterates the view that he has made a clear case for breach of contract.
Decision 1 - 17

B. Sole Arbitrator’s Comments
50. The sole arbitrator briefly commented on the Claimant’s claims on 28 July 2017. Specifically,
the sole arbitrator:
(a) confirmed that he is familiar with LCIA procedures and clarified that “his
ignorance of the LCIA procedures that apply when governing an UNCITRAL
award only extends to the format of the award itself”;
(b) indicated that he acted with scrupulous impartiality in determining the
jurisdictional issues;
(c) confirmed his findings on UK employment laws;
(d) drew attention to s. 29 of the Act with regards to the request for refund of his
fees; and
(e) stated that he was not prejudging the merits of the main claim by his
statement that the Claimant would have difficulties in proving breach of
contract, but rather made the comment “in a spirit of openness and fairness,
particularly in light of the fairly modest amount at stake.”
51. In his email dated 17 August 2017, the sole arbitrator stated that he “ha[s] had no unilateral
communication with either party and in fact notified the parties at the outset of the case […] of the
importance of all communications being inter partes”. On 13 September 2017, he further clarified, in
response to the Claimant’s arguments, that he never made an order of costs in this case, reserving any
such question for the Final Award.
Decision 1 - 18

C. Respondent’s Comments
52. The Respondent submits that the challenge is without merit, as contended in its email of
28 July 2017. In its email of 15 August 2017, the Respondent also denied any allegation of collusion
with the sole arbitrator. Lastly, the Respondent indicated in its emails of 16 August 2017 and
7 September 2017 that it had no further comments on the challenge and did not wish actively to
participate in it.
IV. ANALYSIS
A. Applicable Law and Criteria to be Applied
53. In view of the parties’ explicit choice of London as the seat of arbitration, the Claimant is
correct in identifying English law, together with the Rules, as governing the determination of this
challenge.
54. Article 12(1) of the Rules provides as follows:
Any arbitrator may be challenged if circumstances exist that give rise to justifiable doubts as
to the arbitrator’s impartiality or independence.
55. Under s. 33(1)(a) of the Act, an arbitrator must “act fairly and impartially as between the
parties”. As a corollary, s. 24 of the Act provides that a party may seek the removal of an arbitrator if
“circumstances exist that give rise to justifiable doubts as to his impartiality”. The English courts and
Divisions of the LCIA Court have decided that, since England’s adoption of the European Convention
on Human Rights, the standard provided in the Act also includes the requirement of arbitrator
independence.3
3 LCIA Reference No. 81160, 29 August 2009, at para. 3.3, 27:3 Arbitration International 448; LCIA Reference
No. 81224, 15 March 2010, at paras. 3.4-3.5, 27:3 Arbitration International 465; Lawal v. Northern Spirit Ltd.,
[2003] UKHL 35, at para. 14.
Decision 1 - 19

56. The requirements of impartiality and independence are to be applied from the point of view
of a fair-minded and informed observer. Lord Hope of Craighead, concurring in Porter v. Magill, laid
out the test for reasonable apprehension of bias under English law as being “whether the fair-minded
and informed observer, having considered the facts, would conclude that there was a real possibility
that the tribunal was biased”.4 This test was applied to decide challenge applications under the
UNCITRAL Rules in arbitral proceedings seated in London.5 It has also been applied by LCIA Divisions
acting under the LCIA Rules.6
57. In a recent decision, the English commercial court summarized as follows the main authorities
relating to s. 24 of the Act, including as regards the notion of the “fair-minded and informed observer”:
(1) The common law test for apparent bias is reflected in section 24 – see, for example,
Laker Airways v FLS Aerospace [1999] 2 Lloyds Rep 45, per Rix J at [48]; A v B [2011] 2 Lloyds
Rep 591 per Flaux J at [21]-[29]; Sierra Fishing Co & Others v Farran & Others [2015] EWHC
140 (Comm), [2015] Lloyds Law Reports per Popplewell J at [51];
(2) The common law test under section 24 is whether “the fair minded and informed
observer, having considered the facts, would conclude that there was a real possibility that
the tribunal was biased” – see Porter v Magill [2002] AC 357 per Lord Hope at [103]; Helow v
Secretary of State for the Home Department [2008] UKHL 62, [2008] 1 WLR 2416, per Lord
Hope at [1]-[3];
(3) Such a fair minded and informed observer, although not a lawyer, is assumed to be in
possession of all the facts which bear on the question and expected to be aware of the way in
which the legal profession operates in practice – see Rustal v Gill & Dufus [2001] 1 Lloyd's Law

58. The undersigned has applied the foregoing principles in deciding the challenge.
B. Admissibility
59. The first question that arises is whether the Claimant’s challenge was submitted within the
time limits set out in Article 13(1) of the Rules. This article reads as follows:
A party that intends to challenge an arbitrator shall send notice of its challenge within 15 days
after it has been notified of the appointment of the challenged arbitrator, or within 15 days
after the circumstances mentioned in articles 11 and 12 became known to that party.
60. Most of the grounds raised by the Claimant in support of his challenge relate to the Partial
Award issued by the sole arbitrator on 13 July 2017 and to an email sent by the sole arbitrator on the
same day. Given that the challenge was submitted on 27 July 2017, notice of the challenge was sent
within the prescribed limits insofar as these grounds are concerned.
61. The Claimant’s challenge also impugns procedural decisions made by the sole arbitrator in the
course of the proceedings, well before the issuance of the Partial Award. For example, the Claimant
depicts the sole arbitrator’s decision to bifurcate the proceedings as evidencing a lack of impartiality
on his part. This decision, which is rooted in PO 1, was communicated to the parties in several emails,
most notably his emails dated 21 April and 3 May 2017, in which the sole arbitrator informed the
parties that he would first rule on the jurisdictional objections.

62. The Claimant received PO 1 and was copied on these emails. He therefore knew about these
circumstances more than 15 days before he submitted his challenge. Accordingly, pursuant to
Article 13(1) of the Rules, these circumstances cannot serve as a basis for the challenge.
63. Having noted the timeliness issue that arises with some of the grounds for the challenge, the
undersigned will nevertheless address these circumstances on the merits in the section below.
C. Merits
64. The undersigned addresses in turn the four categories of grounds raised by the Claimant in
support of his challenge, namely those relating to (1) the arbitrator’s experience and expertise; (2) his
procedural decisions; (3) allegedly incorrect statements, and omissions in his Partial Award; and
(4) the substance of the Partial Award.
1. Arbitrator’s Experience and Expertise
65. The sole arbitrator did indicate in his email of 13 July 2017, that “he was admittedly not
familiar with the LCIA procedures when the proceedings are under the UNCITRAL Rules”. However,
this statement has to be put in its proper context. First, the sole arbitrator did not state that he was
unfamiliar with the Rules themselves, as the Claimant argues, but rather that he was “not familiar with
the LCIA procedures” (emphasis added) under those Rules. The sole arbitrator clarified, in his email of
28 July 2017, that he was referring in his statement to his lack of familiarity with “the form and format
of the award itself” (emphasis added), not with the substance of the Rules.
66. The record of the proceedings tends to show that the arbitrator is knowledgeable about the
conduct of an arbitration under the Rules. The arbitrator frequently made reference to the Rules in
the course of the arbitration, and it was never suggested, during the proceedings, that he misapplied
the Rules. In sum, the undersigned cannot accept the submission that the Claimant consented to the
Decision 1 - 22

appointment of the sole arbitrator based on false information about the latter’s experience and
expertise.
67. In any event, the arbitrator’s stated lack of familiarity with the LCIA procedures as regards the
form of awards when an arbitration is conducted under the UNCITRAL Rules, and his purported failure
to inform the parties of that fact before his appointment, do not give rise to justifiable doubts as to
his impartiality or independence. A fair minded and informed observer, having considered the facts as
a whole, would not see a real possibility that the sole arbitrator was biased due to these
circumstances.
2. Procedural Decisions
68. Article 17(1) of the Rules gives broad discretionary powers to the arbitrator regarding
procedural decisions, so long as the parties are treated with equality and are given a reasonable
opportunity to present their case:
Subject to these Rules, the arbitral tribunal may conduct the arbitration in such manner as it
considers appropriate, provided that the parties are treated with equality and that at an
appropriate stage of the proceedings each party is given a reasonable opportunity of
presenting its case. The arbitral tribunal, in exercising its discretion, shall conduct the
proceedings so as to avoid unnecessary delay and expense and to provide a fair and efficient
process for resolving the parties’ dispute.
69. This power, combined with the criteria set out above to determine challenges based on an
alleged lack of impartiality or independence of the arbitrator, show that mere dissatisfaction with the
procedural decisions of an arbitrator is insufficient to ground a challenge.8 As regards procedural
decisions, the arbitrator must exercise his or her discretion fairly and impartially, and treat the parties
8 LCIA Reference No. 7990, 21 May 2010, at para. 4.1, 27:3 Arbitration International 473.
Decision 1 - 23

with equality. With this in mind, the undersigned turns to consider the Claimant’s various arguments
regarding the arbitrator’s procedural decisions.
70. First, the Claimant points to the arbitrator’s failure to establish the timetable of the entire
case in accordance with Article 17(2) of the Rules. This Article reads as follows:
As soon as practicable after its constitution and after inviting the parties to express their views,
the arbitral tribunal shall establish the provisional timetable of the arbitration. The arbitral
tribunal may, at any time, after inviting the parties to express their views, extend or abridge
any period of time prescribed under these Rules or agreed by the parties.
71. Contrary to the Claimant’s suggestion, the arbitrator’s decision as regards the timetable
complies with Article 17(2). While this Article indicates that the “tribunal shall establish the provisional
timetable of the arbitration”, it does not require that this timetable at once cover the entire
proceedings. Indeed, it is open to the Tribunal and the parties to plan the first steps of the arbitration,
and leave the remainder for subsequent determination. This possibility falls within the discretion
provided to the Tribunal under Article 17(1).
72. In the present case, the arbitrator consulted the parties before issuing PO 1. At the relevant
time, the Claimant did not object to the provisional timetable proposed for the case. He participated
in the conference call, on 19 January 2017, during which the timeline was discussed and he had an
opportunity subsequently to provide comments on a draft of PO 1. In the undersigned’s opinion, the
approach of the sole arbitrator in establishing the provisional timetable would not be seen by a fair
minded and informed observer as displaying a lack of impartiality or independence.9
73. Second, the Claimant points to the arbitrator’s decision to bifurcate the proceedings and to
rule first on the Respondent’s jurisdictional pleas. It is first noted in this respect that the possibility of

making separate rulings on jurisdiction and on the merits of a case is specifically provided for in
Article 23(3) of the Rules:
The arbitral tribunal may rule on a plea referred to in paragraph 2 [a plea that the arbitral
tribunal does not have jurisdiction] either as a preliminary question or in an award on the
merits. The arbitral tribunal may continue the arbitral proceedings and make an award,
notwithstanding any pending challenge to its jurisdiction before a court. [Emphasis added.]
74. This possibility is also reflected in Article 34(1) of the Rules, which provides that “[t]he arbitral
tribunal may make separate awards on different issues at different times”.
75. In this case, the fact that both parties initially expressed the wish to resolve the entire dispute
on a summary basis10, did not preclude the arbitrator from suggesting a different course once the case
had evolved and jurisdictional objections had formally been raised. Most certainly his decision in this
respect falls within the discretion he enjoys under Articles 17(1) and 23(3) of the Rules. Nor did it
preclude the Respondent eventually from agreeing with such a suggested course of action.
76. It appears from the record that the possibility of bifurcating the proceedings was raised by the
sole arbitrator on 16 and 17 January 2017, and it was formally and clearly notified to the parties in
PO 1. As explained previously, the Claimant had the opportunity to comment on this Order before it
was formalized, but he failed to do so.
77. The Claimant also failed to raise an objection when, on 21 April 2017, the arbitrator advised
the parties that as per PO 1 he had decided to rule on the jurisdictional objections first, without
holding a hearing. The Claimant even made additional submissions on the admissibility of his claims
on 9 May 2017, thus fully participating in the bifurcated proceedings. When the arbitrator confirmed,
once again on 8 June 2017, that he would rule on the jurisdictional pleas only, the Claimant did not

object. It is only on 19 June 2017, after his counsel had withdrawn from the case, that the Claimant
started to object to the bifurcation of the proceedings.
78. In sum, there is no indication in the record that the decision to bifurcate was made otherwise
than in an impartial and independent manner.
79. The Claimant also made the very serious allegation that the sole arbitrator and the
Respondent colluded, or at least engaged in ex parte communications, on the opportunity of
bifurcating the proceedings. The Respondent denied this allegation, and the sole arbitrator affirmed
unequivocally that he “ha[s] had no unilateral communication with either party”. Nothing in the record
supports the claim of collusion and the undersigned rejects it.
80. Lastly, the Claimant takes issue with the arbitrator’s decision to address, in his Partial Award,
the merits of claims that had been withdrawn, thus wasting the parties’ resources. While it may well
be that it was unnecessary for the sole arbitrator to address these grounds in detail, the decision to
do so does not, in itself, evidence a lack of impartiality or independence. Indeed, it may be interpreted
as intending to reassure the Claimant that his decision to withdraw those claims was sound.
81. The undersigned concludes that nothing in the impugned procedural decisions of the sole
arbitrator would lead a fair minded and informed observer to conclude that these decisions raise
justifiable doubts as to the arbitrator’s impartiality and independence.
3. Incorrect Statements and Omissions in the Partial Award
82. The same can be said of the allegedly incorrect statements contained in the Partial Award, or
the various omissions noted by the Claimant.

83. First, the Claimant points to the arbitrator’s statement at paragraph 20 of the Partial Award
that while “[the Claimant] retained English solicitors, [B], […] it appears that their retainer was
terminated by [the Claimant] shortly before this Award was published”. The Claimant protests that it
was his counsel that withdrew from the case.
84. The record contains an email dated 9 August 2017 from the Claimant’s former counsel stating
that they “could no longer continue to represent [him] because of a conflict of interest”. An earlier
email dated 20 June 2017 from the Claimant on which the sole arbitrator was copied indicates that,
at least from the Claimant’s perspective, it was his counsel who chose to withdraw from the file, not
the Claimant who terminated his retainer.
85. Be that as it may, this factual mistake regarding the Claimant’s legal representation is not
material and does not, in itself, show any lack of impartiality or independence on the part of the sole
arbitrator. The undersigned concludes that, at worse, this was an innocuous honest mistake that a fair
minded and informed observer would not see as suggestive of bias.
86. Second, the Claimant takes issue with the fact that the account of the proceedings in the
Partial Award ends on 8 June 2017 and therefore does not reflect the concerns he continued to raise
until 12 July 2017. However, this is a function of the sole arbitrator having notified the parties, on
8 June 2017, that he was proceeding to draft his Partial Award on jurisdiction. By then, both parties
had had a full opportunity to comment on the jurisdictional pleas and the sole arbitrator was justified
in considering this part of the case closed.
87. In any event, a decision or award does not have exhaustively to list and summarize any and
all communications between the parties and the Tribunal, especially when they are not directly

relevant to the issue to be determined in the decision or award. In sum, therefore, this omission does
not give rise to any justifiable doubt as to the sole arbitrator’s impartiality or independence.
88. Lastly, the Claimant takes issue with the fact that the Partial Award mentions the
Respondent’s request for costs, whereas no mention is made in the award of his own request for costs.
It appears that this request was made on 19 June 2017, and therefore after the sole arbitrator had
notified the parties that he would proceed to draft his Partial Award on jurisdiction. In any event, and
more to the point, the sole arbitrator has made no decision as to costs thus far, and made clear in his
Partial Award that he is reserving this issue for the Final Award. Accordingly, the sole arbitrator will,
in the fullness of time, be in a position to take account of the requests for costs of both the Claimant
and the Respondent. For the time being, his failure expressly to mention the Claimant’s request for
costs in the Partial Award does not give rise to justifiable doubts as to his impartiality or independence.
4. Alleged errors as to UK Law and Pre-Judgment of the Merits
89. The last ground for the challenge is the alleged distortion, by the arbitrator, of the laws
governing the case, and the contention that he pre-judged the breach of contract claim.
90. As regards the first point, it does not fall upon the undersigned to review the merits of the
sole arbitrator’s decision or to sit in appeal of his jurisdictional ruling. To quote from a previous
challenge decision, it is not “a function of the LCIA Court to review the conclusions (whether of fact or
of law) of an arbitrator’s award in order to determine whether or not such conclusions were properly
supported by the parties’ submissions or the evidence adduced”.11 The Claimant must show that a fair
minded and informed observer would consider that these aspects of the sole arbitrator’s Partial Award

give rise to justifiable doubts as to his impartiality or independence. In the opinion of the undersigned,
the Claimant has failed to do so.
91. The Claimant first takes issue with the sole arbitrator’s decision that the Agreement is not a
contract of employment and that he does not enjoy protection under UK laws, including the
Employment Rights Act.
92. This ruling falls directly within the sole arbitrator’s jurisdiction, including his jurisdiction to rule
on his own jurisdiction under Article 23(1) of the Rules. It is not the role of the undersigned to
determine whether his decision on such a question is correct or not. The Claimant alleges no other
circumstance in relation to that decision that is said to give rise to justifiable doubts as to the sole
arbitrator’s impartiality or independence.
93. Second, the Claimant contends that the arbitrator pre-judged the merits of his claim for
breach of contract, by stating a provisional view and indicating that the Claimant would face evidential
difficulties in proving his claim.
94. It is possible to conceive of circumstances where the expression of a strong opinion on the
merits of a claim before the arbitrator has heard the parties’ arguments might give rise to justifiable
doubts as to an arbitrator’s impartiality or independence. That is not the case here. At paragraph 65
of his Partial Award, the sole arbitrator “ma[d]e clear that [his] view [wa]s provisional, and there may
well be evidence that supports the breach of contract claim”. I conclude, as other LCIA Divisions have
concluded in similar circumstances, that such an expression of preliminary views cannot serve as the
basis for a challenge.12

95. The sole arbitrator having made clear that the view he expressed was provisional, there is no

5. Conclusion
96. For reasons set out above, the undersigned is of the view that none of the grounds for
challenge raised by the Claimant, taken individually or as a whole, gives rise to justifiable doubts as to
the arbitrator’s impartiality or independence. To the contrary, the record shows that the arbitrator
acted fairly and impartially at every step of the proceedings.
V. COSTS
97. The last issue to be addressed is the determination and allocation of costs in relation to this
challenge. In the absence of submissions by the parties regarding this question, the undersigned
prefers to defer the question to the arbitrator.13
98. The Claimant has requested a refund of the fees paid to the arbitrator. This claim being
dependent on the outcome of the challenge, it must necessarily fail in light of the undersigned’s
decision to dismiss the challenge, this being determined leaving altogether aside the question of
whether the undersigned would have jurisdiction to deal with such a request.
